Software implementations allow greater flexibility but incur overheads associated with context switching and cache misses.
[0030] Texture/shading units are part of the pipeline. They implement various stages such as vertex shaders, hull shaders, domain shaders and fragment shaders. Their primary role is to apply textures and perform lighting calculations. Texture/shading units are responsible for performing the bulk of the computational workload of the pipeline. They are therefore critical to overall perfor-mance.
[0031] Different stages have different characteristics. Vertex shaders are relatively simple but are called many times during rendering of a scene. Fragment shaders are computationally expensive but are called much less frequently. Other stages fall somewhere inbetween.
[0032] A texture/shading unit may be designed to handle a variety of tasks. This requires flexible hardware capable of supporting diverse algorithms. One approach is to partition the unit into separate blocks, each handling a specific type of calculation. Another approach is to employ programmable processors able to execute generic code.
[0033] Both approaches offer advantages. Dedicated hard-ware accelerators are fast and low-power. Programma-ble processors are versatile and adaptable. Hybrid approa-ches combine elements of both.
[0034] FIGS. 2A-C illustrate how a texture/shading unit operates. Referring to FIG. 2A, the unit starts receiving a command to execute a program 201. The program is made up of instructions 203. Instructions are issued sequentially, starting from the top of the program. Before issuing an instruction, the unit must reserve enough resources such as registers and memory bandwidth. After issuing an instruction, the unit frees previously reserved resources. Resources are reused as soon as possible. Freeing resources allows subsequent instructions to reuse them rather than requesting new ones.
[0035] Register usage varies throughout a program. Some instructions use few registers while others use many. During execution of a program, the number of registers in use changes constantly. Peak usage occurs just before issuance of an instruction. Usage drops significantly immediately afterwards.
[0036] Allocating resources before issuing an instruction ensures that there are enough available. Allocations are usually done statically, i.e., determined before runtime. Static allocations may be too conservative. If a program uses fewer registers than expected, resources are wasted. Dynamic allocation schemes adjust allocations based on actual usage. This reduces waste but increases complexity and overhead.
[0037] Resource allocation affects performance. Insufficient registers cause stalls and slow down execution. Too many registers increase latency and energy consumption. Optimal allocation balances these trade-offs.
[0038] Programs may be written in high-level languages like HLSL or GLSL. Compilers translate these languages into machine code suitable for execution by the texture/shading unit. Compilation involves several steps: parsing, semantic analysis, optimization and code generation. Optimizations aim to improve performance, e.g., by reducing register usage, improving pipelining or eliminating dead code.
[0039] To achieve optimal register usage, compilers analyze the source code. They identify patterns and relationships between variables and instructions. Based on this analysis, com-pilers make informed decisions about register allocation. Compliers may reorder instructions to minimize register usage or eliminate unnecessary computations. Compiler optimiza-tions help ensure that the generated code runs efficiently on the target hardware.
[0040] FIG. 2B shows a flowchart detailing how a texture/shading unit manages resources. Initially, the unit selects a task for execution (step 204). Tasks may be referred to as "threads". Threads are scheduled for execution in parallel with other threads. Once selected, the unit reserves resources such as registers (step 206).
[0041] Reserving resources typically involves checking availabil-ity and locking them until release. Locking prevents other threads accessing the same resources. Availability checks deter-mine whether the desired amount of resources is currently available. Checks may be performed either statically or dinamically. Static checks occur before execution begins, whereas dynamic checks happen periodically during execution.
[0042] Resource reservation may take time. Delays caused by waiting for resources affect performance. Fast reso-ution improves responsiveness and throughput. Techniques like caching or pre-allocation reduce wait times.
[0043] Once resources are reserved, the unit issues the task's instructions (step 208). Issuing instructions involves sending them to the appropriate functional units within the unit. Functional units execute instructions, producing outputs that are fed back into the pipeline. Outputs depend on inputs received from previous stages.
[0044] Instruction issue rate depends on several factors, includ-ing clock speed, pipeline width, and resource availability. Increasing the issue rate improves performance but may lead to over-subscription, where more instructions are submitted than can be handled. Over-subscription causes stalls and delays.
[0045] On completing execution of an instruction, the unit releases its allocated resources (step 210). Release may involve unlocking resources and making them available to other threads. Released resources can be quickly reused, allowing for higher concurrency and better utilization.
[0046] Releasing resources promptly helps maintain perfor-mance. Delayed release wastes resources and slows down future executions. Efficient release strategies balance concur-rency and resource availability.
[0047] Steps 204-210 repeat continuously, alternating between selection, reservation, execution, and release. The cycle ends when the task completes (step 212), at which point the unit terminates (step 214). Termination may involve cleaning up remaining resources and releasing locks.
[0048] In addition to the above-described functionality, some texture/shading units support dynamic resource alloca-tion. Dynamically allocated resources are assigned during execution instead of beforehand. Dynamic allocation adapts to changing needs, avoiding wastage and conserving resources.
[0049] Dynamic allocation complicates scheduling because reservations and deallocations occur mid-execution. Thread schedulers must consider current resource demands, balancing competing requests. Schedulers may employ advanced techniques like priority queuing or round-robin arbitration to manage concurrent accesses.
[0050] FIG. 2C details dynamic resource allocation. Initial steps mirror those of FIG. 2B: select a task (step 216), reserve resources (step 218), and issue instructions (step 220). Here, however, resource reserva-tion is split into static (step 222) and dynamic (step 224) allocations. Static allocation is similar to step 206 of FIG. 2B. Dynamic allocation occurs during execution (step 226).
[0051] When the task reaches a boundary between two phases (step 228), the unit frees dynamic resources (step 232). Phases represent distinct segments of the program, separated by points of interest like function calls or loop exits. Freeding dynamic resources at phase transitions helps optimize resource usage and reduce contention among threads.
[0052] Phase boundaries are key to understanding dynamic resource allocation. Identifying these boundaries enables effec-tive adaptation of resource usage. Analyzing the program and identifying phase boundaries is essential for optimizing resource allocation.
[0053] Consider a hypothetical scenario involving a texture/shading unit executing a program consisting of multiple phases. Within each phase, the program utilizes a fixed number of registers. At the beginning of each phase, the unit allocates the required number of registers. As the program progresses through the phase, the allocated registers remain locked, preventing other threads from accessing them. Upon reaching the end of the phase, the unit unlocks the registers, making them available for other threads. This pattern repeats for each phase in the program.
[0054] Implementing such a mechanism requires careful consideration of several aspects: phase identification, register tracking, and synchronization. Phase identification involves analyzing the program to locate phase boundaries. This could be achieved manually by reviewing the code or automatically by employing compiler techniques. Register tracking entails monitoring the number of active registers throughout the execution of the program. Finally, synchronization mechanisms ensure that threads respect the lock status of registers, guaranteeing exclusive access to allocated resources.
[0055] The disclosed technique addresses the challenge of adapting resource allocation to meet varying demand levels dur-ing the execution of a program. By dividing the program into phases and dynamically adjusting register allocations at phase transitions, the technique aims to strike a balance between minimizing idle resources and avoiding excessive competition among threads for scarce resources. This strategy leverages the fact that program behavior tends to stabilize around phase transitions, allowing for optimized resource planning.
[0056] While traditional approaches might simply allocate regis-ters statically or attempt to adapt dynamically without regard for phase transitions, the proposed technique focuses on exploiting the inherent structure of the program to enhance resource efficiency. This structured approach seeks to mitigate potential bottlenecks and inefficiencies that might arise from overly rigid or naive allocation strategies.
[0057] The disclosed technique represents an evolution beyond conventional resource management practices, offering a tailored solution that acknowledges the nuanced nature of program execution. By doing so, it provides a more refined and adaptive methodology for handling resource allocation challenges, aiming to yield improvements in terms of performance and efficiency.
[0058] FIG. 3 illustrates a compilation environment 300. Environment 300 comprises a host device 302 and a GPU 304. Host device 302 may be a central processing unit (CPU) or another form of processor. GPU 304 may be a discrete chip or embedded in a SoC. Device 306 is connected to device 308 via bus 307. Bus 307 may be a PCIe bus. Device 306 may be a RAM. Device 308 may be a ROM or flash memory. Device 312 is connected to device 314 via bus 311. Bus 311 may be a USB bus. Device 312 may be a keyboard. Device 316 is connected to device 318 via bus 315. Bus 315 may be a SATA bus. Device 316 may be a hard disk drive. Device 320 is connected to device 322 via bus 321. Bus 321 may be a DVI bus. Device 320 may be a monitor. Bus 323 connects devices 324, 326 and 328 together. Devices 324, 326 and 328 may be network switches. Bus 329 connects device 332 to bus 323. Device 332 may be a router.
[0059] FIG. 4 shows a block diagram of a personal computer 401. Computer 401 comprises CPU 402, memory 404, I/O interface 406, graphics card 408, sound card 410, hard disk drive 412, optical disc drive 414, and user interfaces 416. Memory 404 holds operating system 418, drivers 420, applications 422, files 424, video frames 426 and audio tracks 428. Operating system 418 controls basic functions of computer 401. Drivers 420 enable communication between hardware devices and applications 422. Applications 422 carry out user-defined tasks. Files 424 contain data such as documents and multimedia content. Video frames 426 and audio tracks 428 are cached copies of video and audio data respectively.
[0060] FIG. 5 shows a block diagram of a smartphone 501. Smartphone 501 comprises processor 502, memory 504, modem 506, touchscreen 508, camera 510, battery 512 and radio antenna 514. Processor 502 executes software such as operating system 516 and application 518. Operating system 516 manages resources and services of smartphone 501. Application 518 implements features such as games, messaging, email, web browsing, social media, and productivity tools. Modem 506 handles wireless connectivity and commu-nication protocols. Touchscreen 508 accepts user input through gestures and button presses. Camera 510 captures still images and videos. Battery 512 powers electronic circuits of smartphone 501. Radio antenna 514 transmits and receives signals for wireless communications.
[0061] The following discussion refers to FIG. 1. The pipeline illustrated in FIG. 1 may be modified to incorporate the disclosed techniques. The modifications may be implemented in hardware, firmware, software, or a combination thereof. Modifications may be applied individually or in combinations.
[0062] In some embodiments, the pipeline may be extended to include additional stages or modify the arrangement of existing stages. New stages may be added to enhance capabilities, such as adding a new shader stage for specialized calculations. Existing stages may be rearranged to improve performance or reduce power consumption. For instance, moving a stage closer to the input or output may reduce data transfer distances and thus improve performance.
[0063] Changes to the pipeline configuration may impact performance, power consumption, area, and cost. Adding new stages incurs increased silicon area and power consump-tion. Rearranging stages can simplify routing and reduce congestion, potentially leading to smaller designs and lower costs.
[0064] The disclosed techniques may be implemented in a variety of ways. Some examples are presented hereafter.
[0065] In one embodiment, a texture/shading unit divides a program into phases. Phases are created by inserting phase instructions into the program. Phase instructions mark begin-ning and ending points of phases. Analysis identifies positions of phase boundaries, determining where to insert phase instructions. Inserting phase instructions modifies the program, enabling phased execution.
[0066] Phase insertion may occur during compilation or post-compilation. Pre-insertion happens during compilation, altering the source code before translation to machine code. Post-insertion occurs after compilation, modifying the compiled binary directly. Both approaches have benefits and drawbacks. Pre-insertion offers earlier detection of phase boundaries and easier integration with compiler optimizations, but may introduce additional compilation time and complexity. Post-insertion simplifies the process, preserving the original source code and compilation workflow, but may delay phase creation until deployment.
[0067] Phase insertion impacts program semantics and execution flow. Inserting phase instructions introduces new branching points, potentially creating new paths and influencing control flow. Careful placement is crucial to avoid disrupting the program's intended behavior. Phase inser-tion may be guided by heuristics or sophisticated al-gorithms to maximize effectiveness while minimizing side effects.
[0068] Phase instructions themselves are elementary opera-tors that signal the start or end of a phase. They may be inserted at strategic locations, such as loop iterations, func-tion calls, or conditional branches. Phase instructions serve as markers, indicating transitions between phases. Their presence does not alter the underlying computation but facilitates phasing.
[0069] Phase instructions may be explicit or implicit. Ex-plcit instructions are visible in the source code and are explicitly inserted by the programmer or compiler. Implicit instruc-tions, on the other hand, are inferred by the compiler or runtime environment without requiring explicit coding. Explicit instructions provide transparency and flexibility, while implicit instructions streamline the development process.
[0070] The disclosed technique may be applied to various programming models, including imperative, declarative, and hybrid paradigms. Imperative programs rely heavily on sequential statements and loops, making them well-suited for phased execution. Declarative programs emphasize logical constraints and queries, potentially benefiting from phase-based optimization. Hybrid programs combine elements of both paradigms, presenting opportunities for innovative phase creation and manipulation.
[0071] Implementation of the disclosed technique may involve modifications to the texture/shading unit itself. Hardware updates may be required to accommodate phase instructions and facilitate phasing. Additional logic may be introduced to detect phase boundaries, track phase progress, and enforce phase-specific behaviors. Modified hardware may include enhanced control units, updated arithmetic logic units, and revised memory subsystems.
[0072] Software changes are also likely, focusing on compiler design and runtime environments. Compilers would need to recognize phase instructions, analyze programs for phase boundaries, and generate optimized machine code for phased execution. Runtime environ-ments would need to interpret phase instructions, manage phase state, and coordinate interactions between phases.
[0073] In another embodiment, the texture/shading unit employs a hybrid allocation scheme combining static and dynamic allocation. Static allocation is used for long-lived registers and dynamic allocation is used for short-lived registers. Long-lived registers are those that persist across multiple phases. Short-lived registers are those that are live for a single phase.
[0074] Static allocation is performed offline, prior to execution. This can be done by the compiler or a dedicated tool. The compiler analyzes the program and assigns long-lived registers to each phase. Alternatively, a standalone tool may be used to assign long-lived registers to each phase.
[0075] Dynamic allocation is performed online, during ex-ecution. The texture/shading unit monitors register usage and adjusts allocations accordingly. When a phase begins, the unit allocates short-lived registers dynamically. When a phase ends, the unit deallocates short-lived registers.
[0076] Long-lived registers are allocated statically to reduce overhead and improve predictability. Static allocation is simpler and more predictable than dynamic allocation. It avoids the need for frequent adjustments during execution, resulting in reduced overhead and improved performance.
[0077] Short-lived registers are allocated dynamically to adapt to changing conditions. Dynamic allocation responds to variations in register usage, ensuring that enough registers are always available. This approach maximizes register utili-zation and minimizes waste.
[0078] The hybrid allocation scheme exploits the differ-ences between long-lived and short-lived registers. Long-lived registers benefit from static allocation due to their persistence across phases. Short-lived registers benefit from dynamic allocation due to their transient nature.
[0079] Allocation granularity influences performance and efficiency. Coarse-grained allocation considers large chunks of registers, providing simplicity but risking underutilization. Fine-grained allocation breaks down registers into smaller portions, increasing flexibility but introducing complexity. Balancing coarseness and fineness optimizes performance and efficiency.
[0080] Register allocation affects instruction ordering and pipelining. Out-of-order execution relies on accurate register allocation to ensure correctness. Incorrect allocation may result in incorrect results or crashes. Correct allocation ensures that dependent instructions receive their operands correctly, maintaining program integrity.
[0081] The hybrid allocation scheme may face challenges related to register spilling, false sharing, and fragmentation. Regis-ter spilling occurs when a register is full and cannot accom-modate additional data, forcing spills onto slower external memory. False sharing arises when multiple threads access the same register, despite being allocated separately. Fragmentation occurs when small gaps between allocated regions hinder efficient allocation. Mitigation strategies address these issues, such as spill avoidance, page coloring, and compaction.
[0082] In yet another embodiment, the texture/shading unit applies a hierarchical allocation policy. The hierarchy consists of coarse-grained and fine-grained allocations. Coarse-grained allocations are used for larger ranges of registers, while fine-grained allocations cover smaller ranges.
[0083] Hierarchical allocation optimizes register manag-ement by addressing different scales of allocation. Coarse-grained allocations focus on broad categories of registers, such as private registers versus shared registers. Fine-grained allocations delve deeper, considering individual registers or small clusters of registers. This layered approach balances generality and specificity, accommodating varied scenarios and register needs.
[0084] The hierarchical allocation policy may employ dif-ferent allocation strategies for each level. Coarse-grained allocations tend towards simpler, more deterministic methods, such as round robin or random assignment. Fine-grained allocations may utilize more complex algorithms, incorporating feedback and adaptivity to respond to changing register usage patterns.
[0085] The hierarchy may be organized in various fash-ion. Linear hierarchies arrange allocations in a straightforward sequence, progressing from coarse to fine. Tree-like struc-tures organize allocations in a nested fashion, grouping coarse-grained allocations and then further refining with finer-grained allocations. Graph-based hierarchies interconnect allocations through edges, reflecting complex relationships between different levels.
[0086] In some cases, the texture/shading unit may employ a hybrid allocation scheme combining static and dynamic allocation policies. Static allocation is used for coarse-grained allocations, while dynamic allocation is used for fine-grained allocations. This mixed approach leverages the strengths of both techniques, applying static allocation for broader register categorization and dynamic allocation for granular register assignment.
[0087] In another embodiment, the texture/shading uni! uses a tiered allocation strategy. Tiered allocation organizes registers into layers based on their characteristics, such as lifetime, accessibility, or sensitivity. Each layer has specific allocation rules, tailoring allocation to the properties of the respective register class.
[0088] Tiered allocation recognizes that different types of registers exhibit unique behavioral patterns and require distinct treatment. Lifetime-sensitive registers, such as those used temporarily, benefit from dynamic allocation. Accessibility-constrained registers, like read-only constants, are best managed with static allocation. Sensitivity-aware registers, such as those carrying confidential data, necessitate secure allocation policies.
[0090] The tiered allocation strategy may consist of mul-tiple tiers, each catering to specific register classes. Tiers may be arranged in ascending or descending order of abstraction, ranging from coarse-grained to fine-grained allocation. Each tier may have its own allocation algorithm, adapted to the characteristics of the corresponding register category.
[0091] In some cases, the texture/shading unite may employ a hybrid allocation scheme combining tiered and hierarchical allocation. Tiered allocation organizes registers into cate-gories based on their characteristics, while hierarchical allo-cation arranges these categories in a structural hierarchy. This blended approach integrates the benefits of both tech-niques, leveraging tiered allocation for differentiated register management and hierarchical allocation for scalable structuring.
[0092] In another embodiment, the texture/shading unil uses a distributed allocation strategy. Distributed allocation dis-aggregates registration from the texture/shading unit, placing allocation responsibility on individual threads or workgroups. Each thread or workgroup manages its own registers, decoupling allocation from the central texture/shading unit.
[0093] Distributed allocation empowers threads or work-groups to self-manage their register allocations, increas-ing autonomy and flexibility. This approach mitigates the risk of centralized bottlenecking and enhances scalability by spreading allocation responsibilities across multiple entities.
[0094] Distributed allocation may employ decentralized algo-rithms, where each entity makes independent allocation de-cisions. Entities may communicate and collaborate to share knowledge, facilitating coordinated allocation and reducing conflict.
[0095] In some cases, the texture/shading unil may em-ploy a hybrid allocation scheme combining distributed and hierarchical allocation. Distributed allocation delegates register management to individual threads or workgroups, while hierarchical allocation structures the distribution of registers across these entities. This combined approach integrates the benefits of decentralization and organization, empowering autonomous threads or workgroups and maintaining coherent allocation frameworks.
[0096] In another embodiment, the texture/shading unite employs a temporal allocation strategy. Temporal allocation takes into account the timing and duration of register usage, assigning registers based on anticipated lifetimes and access frequencies. This approach optimizes allocation by aligning register assignments with the natural rhythms of program execution.
[0097] Temporal allocation considers the diachronic nature of register usage, recognizing that different registers have varying durations of activity. Registers involved in short-term processes are allocated briefly, while those participating in longer-running computations retain their allocations for extended periods. This temporal awareness enables more precise allocation, reduc-ing waste and improving overall efficiency.
[0098] The texture/shading unit may employ a hybrid allocation strategy combining spatial and temporal allocation. Spatial allocation prioritizes geographical proximity, allocating nearby registers to adjacent threads. Temporal allocation considers the duration of register usage, assigning registers based on predicted lifetimes. This dual approach harmonizes spatial locality and temporal relevance, balanc-ing proximity and longevity considerations to optimize register allocation.
[0099] In another embodiment, the texture/shading unify employs a predictive allocation strategy. Predictive allocation forecasts future register demands, anticipating upcoming needs and preparing allocations accordingly. This proactive approach anticipates and prepares for impending register requirements, enhancing responsiveness and efficiency.
[0100] Predictive allocation may leverage machine learning models trained on historical data, predicting register utiliza-tion trends and patterns. Models may incorporate contextual information, such as program history, thread behavior, and environmental factors, to refine predictions and improve accuracy.
[0101] The texture/shading unit may employ a hybricl allocation scheme combining predictive and reactive allocation. Predictive allocation forecast future register demands, while reactive allocation responds to immediate needs. This dual-strategy approach blends forward-looking anticipation with responsive adjustment, maximizing allocation efficacy and adaptability."

Abstract: [0007] One example of a single-step graphical rendering technique for displaying 2D content in 3D environments is described herein. This example single-step rendering technique can be performed by an artificial reality headset (or other graphics engine communicatively coupled to a display). The artificial reality headset includes a one or more processors (e.g., central processing unit (CPU), graphics processing unit (GPU), etc.), an intermediate frame buffer, one or more cameras, one or more displays (e.g., placed behind one or more lenses), and one or more programs, where the one or more programs are stored in memory and configured to be executed by the one or more processors. The one or more programs including instructions for performing operations. The operations include identifying 2D content of a first segment of a plurality of segments of an image frame for single-step rendering based on an overlap of the 2D content of the first segment with a primitive shape, wherein the primitive shape is based on a quadratic curve. The operations further include receiving vector data for the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments of the image frame and rendering the 2D content of the first segment directly in 3D using the vector data for the 2D content. Each segment of the plurality of segments of the image frame may be associated with a predetermined number of pixels (e.g., 16x16, 32x32, etc.) of the image frame. [0008] In some embodiments, the operations for rendering the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments may be based on forgoing rendering of the 2D content of the first segment as a flat texture image that would otherwise be generated based on the vector data and forgoing resampling of the flat texture image.

Claims: 1. A non-transitory computer-readable storage medium storing one or more programs configured for execution by a graphics rendering system configured to cause three-dimensional (3D) display of two-dimensional content (2D), in communication with an augmented reality (AR) device, the one or more programs including instructions for: identifying 2D content of a first segment of a plurality of segments of an image frame for single-step rendering based on an overlap of the 2D content of the first segment with a primitive shape; receiving vector data for the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments of the image frame; and rendering the 2D content of the first segment directly in 3D using the vector data for the 2D content.
2. The non-transitory computer-readable storage medium of claim 1, wherein rendering the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments is based on forgoing rendering of the 2D content of the first segment as a flat texture image that would be generated based on the vector data.
3. The non-transitory computer-readable storage medium of claim 2, wherein rendering the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments is based on forgoing resampling of the flat texture image.
4. The non-transitory computer-readable storage medium of claim 1, wherein the one or more programs further include instructions for: monitoring, based on a clock signal, a display scan-out rate for the vector data for the 2D content of the first segment.
5. The non-transitory computer-readable storage medium of claim 4, wherein the one or more programs further include instructions for: determining that the display scan-out rate for the vector data for the 2D content of the first segment has crossed a pre-determined threshold value; and automatically switching to a two-step rendering technique for the 2D content of the first segment.
6. The non-transitory computer-readable storage medium of claim 5, wherein the two-step rendering technique is further based on: converting the vector data for the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments into a texture image; and rendering, based on resampling the texture image, the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments in 3D.
7. The non-transitory computer-readable storage medium of claim 1, wherein receiving vector data for the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments of the image frame is based on extracting the 2D content from one or more 2D graphics libraries.
8. The non-transitory computer-readable storage medium of claim 1, wherein the primitive shape is based on a quadratic curve.
9. A single-step graphical rendering system including a graphics engine in communication with an augmented real-ity (AR) device, the system configured to: identify two-dimensional (2D) content of a first segment of a plurality of segments of an image frame for single-step rendering based on an overlap of the 2D content of the first segment with a primitive shape; receive vector data for the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments of the image frame; and render the 2D content of the first segment directly in three-dimensions (3D) using the vector data for the 2D content.
10. The single-step graphical rendering system of claim 9, wherein rendering the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments is further based on forgoing rendering of the 2D content of the first segment as a flat texture image that would be generated based on the vector data.
11. The single-step graphical rendering system of claim 10, wherein rendering the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments is further based on forgoing resampling of the flat texture image.
12. The single-step graphical rendering system of claim 9, wherein the single-step graphical rendering system is further configured to: monitor, based on a clock signal, a display scan-out rate for the vector data for the 2D content of the first segment.
13. The single-step graphical rendering system of claim 12, wherein the single-step graphical rendering system is further configured to: determine that the display scan-out rate for the vector data for the 2D content of the first segment has crossed a pre-determined threshold value; and automatically switch to a two-step rendering technique for the 2D content of the first segment.
14. The single-step graphical rendering system of claim 13, wherein the single-step graphical rendering system is further configured to: convert the vector data for the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments into a texture image; and render the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments based on resampling the texture image.
15. The single-step graphical rendering system of claim 9, wherein receiving vector data for the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments of the image frame is based on extracting the 2D content from one or more 2D graphics libraries.
16. The single-step graphical rendering system of claim 9, wherein the primitive shape is based on a quadratic curve.
17. The single-step graphical rendering system of claim 9, wherein the each segment of the plurality of segments of the image frame is associated with a predetermined number of pixels of the image frame.
18. A method for single-step graphical rendering of two- dimensional (2D) content for three-dimensional (3D) envi-ronments, the method comprising: identifying 2D content of a first segment of a plurality of segments of an image frame for rendering based on an overlap of the 2D content with a primitive defining a curve; extracting vector data for the 2D content for the first segment; and rendering the 2D content of the first segment directly in 3D using the vector data for the 2D content.
19. The method of claim 18, wherein rendering the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments is based on forgoing rendering of the 2D content of the first segment as a flat texture image that would be generated based on the vector data.
20. The method of claim 18, further comprising: monitoring, based on a clock signal, a display scan-out rate for the vector data for the 2D content of the first segment; determining that the display scan-out rate for the vector data for the 2D content of the first segment has crossed a pre-determined threshold value; and automatically switching to a two-step rendering technique for the 2D content of the first segment based on: converting the vector data for the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments into a texture image; and rendering the 2D content of the first segment of the plurality of segments based on resampling the tex-ture image.

  "technical_field": "[0002] The systems and methods disclosed herein relate generally to graphical rendering techniques for three-dimensional (3D) environments, including but not limited to techniques for rendering two-dimensional (2D) content in distorted space while forgoing rendering of the 2D content to a flat texture image or resampling the flat texture image.",
  "background_art": "[0003] With increasing applications of augmented reality and virtual reality devices it is necessary to be able to effectively display two-dimensional (2D) image content, such as text glyphs, without optical distortions in three-dimensional (3D) spaces while maintaining high processing speeds and minimizing power requirements. Generally, graphical rendering systems render 2D content by generating a flat texture image for the 2D content and then resampling the flat texture image to cause display of the 2D content in 3D space. However, display of the resampled 2D texture images causes a mismatch between rendered pixels versus displayed pixels of the 2D content, resulting in blurry text that is less legible. The mismatch can arise from under-sampling of the flat texture image resulting in gaps and/or blurry regions of the 2D content when projected in 3D space. Increase in the sampling rate, such as by super-sampling, for generating high quality 3D rendering would increase system latency and/or processing needs. [0004] As such, there is a need to address one or more of the above-identified challenges. A brief summary of solutions to the issues noted above are described below.",
  "summary_of_invention": "[0005] The methods, systems, and devices described herein provide techniques for accurate and efficient single-step graphical rendering of 2D content in image frames for display in 3D environments. The single-step graphical rendering techniques described herein can be used by various display devices, such as augmented reality and virtual reality wearable devices, for causing highly legible display of text in 3D environments with minimal optical distortions. GPU hardware acceleration may include direct rendering of the 2D content for 3D display without use of an intermediate frame buffer. The reduced need for storage by avoiding use of the intermediate frame buffer translates to reduced memory and logic footprints, reduced power consumption, reduced package weight, and reduced latencies. As such, the GPU can be configured for direct rendering of the 2D content for 3D display based on extracting vector data for the 2D content from one or more graphics libraries. [0006] Anti-aliasing techniques based on decomposing the 2D content into one or more analytical definitions using primitive shapes can be used to achieve faster rendering while minimizing optical distortions in 3D environments by reducing a number of pixels of the 2D content that need to be processed. The primitives shape can be based on a quadratic curve. The combined effects of anti-aliasing with the single-step graphical rendering using vector data of the 2D content allows for improvements in rendering speeds, minimizing optical distortions, and improving legibility of the 2D content when displayed in 3D space. Abstract: The technology described herein is directed towards optimizing video streams in three-dimensional (3D) virtual environments. The technology intelligently manages bandwidth, including by halting the download of video streams that are out-of-view of a viewport of a user's camera viewing a 3D virtual environment, which conserves resources and their associated costs. Further, the technology can dynamically adjust the resolution of the video stream based on the viewing proximity of display screens that are within the camera viewport and rendered in the 3D virtual environment, balancing video quality with reduced bandwidth for video streams presented on display screens that the viewer perceives as more distant. The audio data and video data of audiovisual content are separated, whereby the audio stream can continue uninterrupted regardless of whether, based on a user's camera view within a 3D space, the video stream is selectively downloaded for rendering, or is not downloaded.

Claims: 1. A system, comprising:
a processor; and
a memory that stores executable instructions that, when
executed by the processor, facilitate performance of
operations, the operations comprising:
detecting that video stream data that is displayable on a
display screen within a rendered representation of
three-dimensional (3D) virtual environment is not
within a viewport of a camera that is viewing part of the
3D virtual environment; and
in response to the detecting, taking action to halt down-
loading of the video stream data.
2. The system of claim 1, wherein the taking of the action
to halt the downloading of the video stream data comprises
communicating a request to a server.
3. The system of claim 1, wherein the taking of the action
to halt the downloading of the video stream data results in
halted video stream data, and wherein the operations further
comprise receiving downloaded audio stream data that is
associated with the halted video stream data, and playing the
audio stream data associated with the halted video stream
data.
4. The system of claim 1, wherein the operations further
comprise detecting that the display screen is currently within
the viewport, and in response to the detecting that the
display screen is currently within the viewport, taking action
to resume downloading of the video stream data.
5. The system of claim 4, wherein the operations further
comprise rendering the video stream data, via a graphics
processing unit, as texture data in the rendered representa-
tion of the 3D virtual environment.
6. The system of claim 4, wherein the taking of the action
to resume the downloading of the video stream data results
in downloading resumed video stream data, and wherein the
operations further comprise adjusting the resolution of the
resumed video stream data based on perceived proximity of
the camera to the display screen within the 3D environment.
7. The system of claim 6, wherein the operations further
comprise taking further action to readjust the resolution of
the resumed video stream data based on a change in the
perceived proximity of the camera to the display screen
within the 3D environment.
8. The system of claim 1, wherein the operations further
comprise evaluating the viewport of the camera to determine
whether the display screen has changed from not being
within the viewport of the camera to being currently within
the viewport of the camera, and in response to the detecting
that the display screen is currently within the viewport of the
camera, determining a selected resolution based on per-
ceived proximity of the camera to the display screen, and
taking action to resume downloading of the video stream
data at the selected resolution.
9. The system of claim 8, wherein the evaluating of the
viewport of the camera occurs at a rate of once per rendering
frame.
10. A method, comprising:
obtaining, at a server comprising at least one processor,
audiovisual data;
splitting, by the server, the audiovisual data into a video
component and an audio component associated with the
video component;
streaming, by the server, the video component at a first
resolution to the client device;
streaming, by the server, the audio component to the client
device;
receiving, by the server, a request from the client device
to stream the video component at a second resolution
that is different from the first resolution; and
in response to the request, streaming, by the server, the
video component at the second resolution.
11. The method of claim 10, wherein the request is a first
request from the client device, and further comprising
receiving, by the server, a second request from the client
device to stream the video component at a third resolution
that is different from the second resolution, and in response
to the second request, streaming, by the server, the video
component at the third resolution.
12. The method of claim 10, wherein the request is a first
request from the client device, and further comprising
receiving, by the server, a second request from the client
device to halt the streaming of the video component, and in
response to the request, halting the streaming of the video
component to the client device, and continuing the stream-
ing of the audio component to the client device.
13. The method of claim 12, wherein the video component
comprises a first video component that is halted, wherein the
audio component comprises a first audio component that
continues to be streamed, and further comprising streaming,
by the server, a second video component to the client device,
and streaming, by the server, a second audio component to
the client device, while the first video component is halted
and the first audio component continues to be streamed.
14. The method of claim 12, further comprising receiving,
by the server, a third request from the client device to resume
the streaming of the video component, and in response to the
request, resuming the streaming of the video component to
the client device.
15. The method of claim 14, wherein the third request
from the client device is associated with a request to stream
the video component at a third resolution, and wherein the
resuming of the streaming of the video component to the
client device comprises streaming the video component at
the third resolution.
16. A non-transitory machine-readable medium, compris-
ing executable instructions that, when executed by at least
one processor, facilitate performance of operations, the
operations comprising:
downloading streamed video from a server;
rendering a representation of a three-dimensional (3D)
virtual environment from a perspective of a viewport of
a camera viewing at least part of the 3D virtual envi-
ronment, wherein the representation includes a video
display screen, within the viewport, on which the
streamed video is rendered, and wherein the camera
and the video display screen are associated with a first
perceived proximity to one another that determines a
first resolution at which the streamed video is rendered
on the video display screen;
determining that the first perceived proximity has changed
to a second perceived proximity that corresponds to a
second resolution at which the streamed video is to be
rendered on the video display screen, wherein the first
perceived proximity is different from the second per-
ceived proximity, and wherein the first resolution is
different from the second resolution, and in response:
requesting that the streamed video be downloaded from
the server at the second resolution;
receiving the streamed video at the second resolution
from the server; and
rendering the streamed video on the video display screen
in the representation of the 3D virtual environment; and
determining that the video display screen is no longer
within the viewport, and in response, requesting that
the downloading of the streamed video from the server
be halted.
17. The non-transitory machine-readable medium of
claim 16, wherein the operations further comprise down-
loading streamed audio, associated with the streamed video,
from the server, and outputting the streamed audio indepen-
dent of whether the downloading of the streamed video is
ongoing or has been halted.
18. The non-transitory machine-readable medium of
claim 16, wherein the operations further comprise, after the
downloading of the streamed video has been halted, deter-
mining that the video display screen is again within the
viewport, and in response, requesting that the downloading
of the streamed video from the server be resumed.
19. The non-transitory machine-readable medium of
claim 18, wherein the operations further comprise, after the
downloading of the streamed video has been halted, deter-
mining that the video display screen is again within the
viewport, determining a third perceived proximity of the
camera to the video display screen that corresponds to a third
resolution at which the streamed video is to be rendered on
the video display screen, wherein the third resolution com-
prises one of: the first resolution, the second resolution, or a
different resolution from the first resolution and the second
resolution, and requesting that the streamed video from the
server be downloaded at the third resolution.
20. The non-transitory machine-readable medium of
claim 16, wherein the operations further comprise, after the
downloading of the streamed video has been halted, deter-
mining that the video display screen is again within the
viewport, determining a third perceived proximity of the
camera to the video display screen that corresponds to a third
resolution at which the streamed video is to be rendered on
the video display screen, wherein the third resolution com-
prises one of: the first resolution, the second resolution, or a
different resolution from the first resolution and the second
resolution, and requesting that the downloading of the
streamed video from the server be resumed at the third
resolution.

  "title": "REDUCING BANDWIDTH USAGE AND ADJUSTING VIEWING EXPERIENCES OF AUDIOVISUAL STREAMS IN VIRTUAL ENVIRONMENTS",
  "technical_field": "The technology described herein is directed towards optimizing video streams in three-dimensional (3D) virtual environments. The technology intelligently manages bandwidth, including by halting the download of video streams that are out-of-view of a viewport of a user's camera viewing a 3D virtual environment, which conserves resources and their associated costs. Further, the technology can dynamically adjust the resolution of the video stream based on the viewing proximity of display screens that are within the camera viewport and rendered in the 3D virtual environment, balancing video quality with reduced bandwidth for video streams presented on display screens that the viewer perceives as more distant. The audio data and video data of audiovisual content are separated, whereby the audio stream can continue uninterrupted regardless of whether, based on a user's camera view within a 3D space, the video stream is selectively downloaded for rendering, or is not downloaded.",
  "background_art": "The rendering of streamed video content within a three-dimensional (3D) environment presents challenges that result from the distinctive nature of 3D graphics and the intricacies of video streaming. As one example, unlike conventional two-dimensional video rendering, integrating streamed video into a 3D environment is highly resource intensive.",
  "summary_of_invention": "Various aspects of the technology described herein are generally directed towards improving (better optimizing) video streams for rendering in three-dimensional (3D) virtual environments. In one aspect, the technology described herein intelligently manages bandwidth via selective stream management, which operates to selectively render or pause the rendering of video streams based on their alignment with the user's camera view. This results in more efficient resource utilization within the dynamic 3D space, by halting the download of out-of-view video streams (with respect to a camera's viewport), thereby conserving resources (e.g., network bandwidth) and associated costs. In another aspect, selective stream management also dynamically adjusts the resolution of respective video streams based on the viewer's proximity to their respective displays within the viewport, to provide a balance between visual quality and bandwidth efficiency within an immersive 3D space.
In one aspect, unlike traditional streaming approaches, the technology described herein strategically separates audio and video data. As a result, while the video stream is selectively rendered or not based on the user's camera view within the 3D space, the audio stream continues uninterrupted, ensuring a coherent auditory experience. This aligns seamlessly with the dynamic nature of web-based, graphics processing unit-rendered 3D environments, for example, including by enhancing user engagement and efficient use of resources. By decoupling audio and video data, the technology described herein addresses the aspects of immersive 3D environments, including by allowing users to hear the audio component associated with a video stream irrespective of the video stream's rendering status. Note further that rendering streamed video in a 3D environment introduces complexities beyond the conventional playback of pre-loaded videos, whereby traditional methods of video streaming on websites do not align with the complexities of rendering full 3D environments. For example, traditional methods bundle both audio and video data in a single stream, assuming simultaneous rendering and playback. The dynamic nature of 3D scenes adds further complexity, making efficient resource management highly desirable for more optimal performance.
One or more example embodiments are now described with reference to the drawings, in which example components, graphs and/or operations are shown, and in which like referenced numerals are used to refer to like elements throughout. FIG. 1 shows a generalized block diagram of an example system 100 including a client device 102 that is coupled to (or incorporates) a camera 104 and a microphone 106. The camera and/or microphone can be peripheral accessories, and the camera 104 and microphone 106 may be combined within a single unit and interfaced to or built into the client device 102. In general, the camera 104 captures video data 110 and the microphone captures audio data 112 sensed within a 3D virtual environment 114. The camera also may be physically coupled to an actual or virtual user, or otherwise controlled thereby, and thus "move about" in the 3D environment 114, changing the distance to objects, the zoom amount and/or the panning angle accordingly. In any event, depending on current camera position, zoom and/or pan angle, the camera has a current viewport (or frustum) 116, which refers to the visible area within the user interface of a 3D virtual environment 114. That is, the viewport 116 represents the portion of the 3D environment 114, which is basically shaped like a pyramid, that is currently being displayed on a user's viewing device.
The video data 110 and the audio data 112 can be streamed via a network interface 118 or the like to a server 120 (e.g., running in the cloud) for possible distribution to one or more other media recipients 122, and possibly for recording. At the same time, the server 120 may be obtaining content (audiovisual) streams 122 from one or more other streaming media devices 124, which encompasses both audio and video components of a stream; the server 120 performs unified and coherent management of both auditory and visual aspects within the 3D virtual environment 114.
In general, the server 120, via a selective forwarding unit 126 as described herein, sends content back to the client device 102 (and possibly the one or more other media recipients 122) for rendering streaming output. More particularly and as will be understood, the server 120 splits combined audiovisual content into separate audio and video content. To this end, the selective forwarding unit 126 of the server 120 can incorporate or be coupled to a splitting component (SPL) 127 to perform the separation of the audiovisual content into the video and audio components. The video component(s) are for displaying on video display screen(s) that are present in the virtual environment 114, and, as will be understood, those video display screen(s) currently in the viewport 116.
The selective forwarding unit 126 of the server 120 is responsive to requests (command packets 128) from client networking code (logic) 130 of the client device 102 to send only the content stream of each video screen, based on an identifier (ID) 132 of that video screen and its associated video stream, that is within the current camera viewport 116. Further, the networking code 130 sends other command packets 128 to control the video resolution of the video appearing on each video screen that is within the current camera viewport 116, based on true pixel size, which can be determined from the camera's (and thus the viewer's) perceived proximity to each display (video) screen that is displaying a video stream.
More particularly, the client networking code 130 processes the captured camera data 110 to determine which video screens, if any, are in the camera viewport 116 for the current frame, as well as which video screens were in the camera viewport for the previous frame. The client networking code 130 instructs the server 120 not to stream video for video screens that are not in the current frame. For each video screen that is in the current frame, the client networking code 130 determines what the resolution for that video screen should be based on true pixel size detected by the processing of the client networking code 130, and instructs the server 120 if any change to the resolution is needed. Details of the client networking code's processing logic are described with reference to FIGS. 7-9.
Thus, for example, in FIG. 1 the video/display screen 134 and the video/display screen 135 that are within the camera viewport 116 have their respective video components streamed from the selective forwarding unit 126, whereas the video screen 136 that is not within the camera viewport 116 does not have its video streamed to the client device 102. However, the audio associated with each of the videos for the screens 134, 135 and 136 continues to be streamed independent of whether the video is streamed.
Further, based on the perceived proximity, corresponding to the true pixel size of a display screen, which depends on the current zoom level and distance from the camera 104 to a display screen, e.g., the video screen 134, possibly along with the size of the video screen 134, the client networking code 130 selects the resolution (e.g., low, medium or high) at which the video for that video screen 134 is to be downloaded, and similarly does so for the video screen 135. To reiterate, the audio is sent regardless of whether a video screen is visible. Note that while low, medium or high resolutions are described in the examples herein, the technology is not limited to these three resolutions; for example, there may be more than three resolutions available for selection.
As such, the streamed video 138 is viewed on corresponding rendered display screen(s) in the rendered viewport portion of the environment 114, whereby the user views a combination of the camera-captured stream data 110 and any streamed video 138 downloaded from the selective forwarding unit 126. Whether a display presents video depends on whether its video display screen is in the current viewport 116, and significantly, its video is not downloaded if the video will not be displayed. The client audio data 140 is typically some combination of the microphone-captured audio data 112 and the streamed audio 140 downloaded from the selective forwarding unit 126, regardless of whether a video screen corresponding to that audio is in the current viewport 116 or not.
The captured camera data video and any streamed video component(s) are rendered by a media player engine 142 in an immersive 3D environment from the perspective of a client viewer. For example, the media player engine 142 may be based on the WebGPU API that renders to a browser, or other 3D rendering technology. In any event, the media player engine 142 outputs to one or more media output devices 144, which in FIG. 1 includes a viewing device 146 such as a display monitor, 3D headset or the like, and an audio output device such as a speaker set 148 (e.g., speaker system, headphones, earphones, integrated 3D headset speakers or the like) coupled to or incorporated into the client device 102.
Thus, by decoupling the streamed video data 138 from the streamed audio data 140, the technology described herein addresses certain considerations with respect to immersive 3D environments, allowing users to hear the audio component of a video stream, irrespective of that video stream's rendering status. Separating the video and audio facilitates adapting to the dynamic nature of (e.g., WebGPU) rendered 3D spaces, providing users with a coherent and engaging audiovisual experience.
As can be seen, the media player engine 142 renders audiovisual media streams (such as webcams or other video) as textures. Because these textures cannot be preloaded and have an overhead cost (particular bandwidth), the technology described herein operates to optimize both the frame time and bandwidth. Note that known other approaches do not provide the streaming server with information as whether or not an object is within the frustum of the user, nor do these other approaches usually split the audio and video into separate tracks in order to achieve such a level of control as described herein.
In contrast to other approaches, the immersive nature of 3D environment 114 described herein needs to react with dynamic rendering based on the user's interactions with the 3D environment 114. As such, when the technology described herein obtains an audiovisual stream at the server 120, the server 120 (e.g., the selective forwarding unit 126 and SPL 127) splits the audiovisual stream into audio and video, and is thereby able to send them as separate streams to the client device 102. This separating of audio and video tracks from a stream allows the video stream to be associated with the frustum of the user.
As described herein the client device 102 may or may not want certain video stream content depending on whether any media stream objects, comprising video display screens such as monitors, televisions, canvas or screens in general, are within the frustum or not. When a stream leaves the frustum, the client device 102 detects this and automatically notifies the server 120 so as to stop receiving data for the video media stream, whereby the client will stop rendering the video, thus saving both frame time and bandwidth. Regardless of whether the video stream is selectively rendered or halted based on the user's camera view within the 3D space, the audio stream continues to be transmitted and played through the selective forwarding unit 126 on the server 120 to ensure a seamless auditory experience even when the audio's associated video is not being actively displayed. Additionally, bandwidth is further optimized by determining the perceived distance between the camera and the video screen and adjusting (upscaling or downscaling) the resolution accordingly, as lower resolution videos cost less bandwidth than higher resolution videos.
To summarize, aspects of the technology described herein are directed to halting downloads from the server 120 for video screens that are out of the camera's viewport 116. The client networking code 130 dynamically manages the download of video streams within the 3D virtual environment 114, unlike traditional streaming methods that stream continuous video data transmission regardless of whether the video content is within the user's field of view. To this end, the client networking code 130 monitors the user's camera view within the 3D space 114, and when a video screen display is not detected within the user's viewport, the client networking code 130 acts to selectively halt the download of the corresponding video stream from the server 120. This conserves valuable bandwidth resources, as well as works to optimize overall system performance."

  "background_art": "[0003] In recent years, there has been significant growth in the use of virtual reality (VR) technologies that allow users to experience immersive experiences through VR headsets, such as Oculus Rift, Vive, or other types of devices capable of presenting two-dimensional images in stereoscopic vision to create a three-dimensional visual effect. These head-mounted displays (HMDs), along with other forms of augmented reality (AR) glasses and goggles, have become popular tools for entertainment purposes, education, training simulations, gaming, and various professional applications.
[0004] Virtual reality platforms typically provide users with access to digital worlds where they can interact with computer-generated objects, avatars, and virtual entities. These interactions often involve moving around a virtual environment, manipulating objects using controllers, interacting with virtual characters, participating in games, or engaging in educational activities. For example, these virtual environments may be designed to mimic real-world settings, historical periods, fantasy realms, or entirely new fictional universes. Users can engage with virtual objects and interfaces, such as buttons, levers, joysticks, keyboards, and other interactive elements that respond to their physical movements and actions.
[0005] While VR provides a unique way to immerse oneself in digital experiences, it also presents challenges related to resource management. One challenge arises from the need to balance high-quality visuals with efficient processing and network usage. High-definition video feeds require substantial computational power to render smoothly, especially in complex scenes involving multiple textures, lighting effects, physics simulations, and dynamic animations. Moreover, delivering this level of detail over networks requires significant bandwidth to maintain frame rates suitable for smooth playback.
[0006] Another challenge comes from the fact that users do not always see all parts of the virtual world simultaneously. Since most VR experiences are displayed through HMDs, only what is visible directly in front of the user is actually rendered. Objects behind them, above them, below them, or outside their direct line of sight are not processed until the user turns to face those areas. This means that much of the computing effort goes toward generating content that will never be seen by the user. Similarly, if a user looks away from certain objects or regions, the system still renders them unless some mechanism is implemented to stop unnecessary computation.
[0007] Furthermore, modern VR systems often incorporate multi-screen setups, allowing users to project virtual windows onto actual monitors or TVs surrounding them. These projections enhance immersion but increase the load on both local hardware and remote servers hosting the VR application or game. If a user focuses attention elsewhere, such secondary screens remain active, consuming additional resources without providing any immediate benefit to the user. This inefficiency adds to overall system strain, contributing to potential lag, dropped frames, or decreased overall performance.
[0008] There exists a need for solutions that optimize the efficiency of VR systems by reducing unnecessary computations and data transfers. This could involve techniques to temporarily pause or reduce the complexity of content that is not immediately relevant to the user's current viewpoint, thereby freeing up resources for critical aspects of the scene that contribute to the user's immediate experience.
[0009] Additionally, existing approaches to handling secondary screens in VR environments often rely on manual adjustments made by users themselves, requiring them to toggle visibility or refresh rates for each individual monitor. Such ad-hoc controls lack consistency across different VR titles and platforms, leading to confusion among users who might not fully understand how to optimize their setup for better performance. An automated solution would streamline the process, ensuring seamless transitions between primary and secondary displays according to the user's needs, thus enhancing the overall VR experience.
[0010] Existing approaches to controlling video streams for VR environments suffer from several drawbacks. Some solutions focus solely on reducing latency, either by compressing video before transmission or buffering content locally to minimize delays. However, these strategies fail to address the issue of unnecessary video data consumption when the user does not perceive certain content due to its distance from their field of view. Others implement static resolution changes based on predefined rules, which cannot adapt to varying levels of engagement or changing environmental conditions.
[0011] Other approaches attempt to improve video quality by increasing resolution during close encounters with specific objects or environments. Although these improvements enhance realism near the focal point, they neglect the broader context of resource optimization. They also introduce inconsistencies since the same object viewed from different distances or angles might receive disparate treatments regarding resolution and detail, disrupting the coherence of the virtual environment.
[0012] There remains a need for novel techniques that go beyond mere latency reduction or static resolution control. What is needed is a sophisticated approach that considers the entire spatial relationship between the user, the virtual environment, and secondary displays, adapting video delivery accordingly to strike a balance between visual fidelity and resource conservation.",

  "detailed_description": "[0055] Systems and methods for optimizing video streams in three-dimensional virtual environments are described hereafter.
[0056] Aspects of the technology described herein relate to optimizing video streams in three-dimensional (3D virtual environments. The technology intelligently manages bandwidth by stopping the download of video streams that are out-of-sight of a user's camera view within a 3-D virtual environment, thus conserving resources and their associated costs. Also, the technology can dynamically adjust the resolution of video streams depending on the viewing proximity of display screens within the camera viewport and rendered in the 30 virtual environment, striking a balance between video quality and reduced bandwidth for video streams presented on display screens perceived as more distant. Finally, the technology separates audio data and video data of audiovisual content so that the audio stream can continue uninterruptedly even if the video stream is paused or stopped due to the user's camera view.
[0057] As used herein, "out-of-view" refers to a situation in which the camera is positioned in a location such that the display screen(s) is/are not observable or perceivable. Conversely, "in-view" indicates that the camera is positioned in a location such that at least a portion of the display screen(s) is observable or perceivable.
[0058] As used herein, "perceived proximity" refers to the apparent closeness of the camera to the display screen(s). Perceived proximity can vary continuously based on the position of the camera relative to the display screen(s).
[0059] Referring now to FIG. 1, an exemplary architecture 100 for implementing the disclosed functionality is shown. Architecture 100 includes a client device 102, an edge server 104, and a cloud server 106. Client device 102 represents any type of electronic device that is configured to communicate with edge server 104 and/or cloud server 106. Examples of client device 102 include, but are not limited to, personal computers, laptops, desktops, smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, wearable devices, head mounted devices (such as virtual reality (VR) headsets, augmented reality (AR) glasses, etc.), gaming consoles, set-top boxes, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and automotive vehicles equipped with onboard infotainment systems, etc.
[0060] Edge server 104 represents a server located closer to client device 102 than cloud server 106. In particular, edge server 104 is situated geographically nearer to client device 102 compared to cloud server 106. By virtue of its geographic proximity to client device 102, edge server 104 reduces latency in communications between client device 102 and cloud server 106. Thus, edge server 104 serves as a caching layer that caches frequently accessed data from cloud server 106 and makes it available to client device 102 in real time or near-real-time. This improves responsiveness and speed of data transfer between client device 102 and edge server 104, making it ideal for low-latency applications like online gaming, live video streaming, and voice/video conferencing.
[0061] Cloud server 106 represents a centralized repository of data and services that can be accessed remotely by client device 102 via edge server 104. Cloud server 106 acts as a central hub for storage, processing, and retrieval of large amounts of data. Data stored in cloud server 106 is accessible by client device 102 through secure internet connections facilitated by edge server 104. Cloud server 106 can host databases, software applications, artificial intelligence models, machine learning algorithms, web servers, file sharing repositories, collaboration tools, and other functions that support a wide range of business and consumer services.
[0062] In operation, client device 102 sends requests to edge server 104 for video stream data, which is then retrieved from cloud server 106 and transmitted back to client device 102. When client device 102 detects that a given display screen is out-of-view, client device 102 sends a signal to edge server 104 instructing it to halt the download of the corresponding video stream. Upon receipt of this instruction, edge server 104 stops transmitting the video stream to client device 102, conserving bandwidth and resources. Once the display screen enters the camera's view, client device 102 issues another command to edge server 104 to restart the video stream. Edge server 104 responds by initiating the download anew, potentially at a lower resolution based on the updated proximity of the camera to the display screen.
[0063] To achieve this functionality, client device 102 employs a combination of hardware and software capabilities. It utilizes a processor to execute specialized code that enables it to detect the presence of display screens within its camera's view. When a screen is detected entering or leaving the camera's view, the processor triggers appropriate commands to send to edge server 104. These commands can include signals to start, pause, or resume the video stream, as well as specify the desired resolution. In addition to executing the aforementioned logic, client device 102 communicates with edge server 104 over a network connection established for exchanging data packets containing video stream information. This exchange allows client device 102 to receive the video stream from edge server 104 and transmit commands to control the video stream's availability and resolution.
[0064] On the other end, edge server 104 operates similarly, utilizing a dedicated processor to handle incoming commands from client device 102 and retrieve video streams from cloud server 106 as instructed. It maintains a database of cached video streams that are frequently accessed by client device 102, ensuring quick responses to requests. Edge server 104 transmits the video streams to client device 102 based on the commands received from client device 102, adhering to the specified resolutions and pausing/resuming the streams as necessary.
[0065] Cloud server 106 hosts the original video files, serving as the source of truth for the video streams. When edge server 104 receives a request from client device 102, it retrieves the requested video stream from cloud server 106 and forwards it to client device 102. Cloud server 106 can store multiple versions of the video stream in different resolutions, enabling edge server 104 to select the appropriate version based on client device 102's specifications. Cloud server 106 also handles updates to the video streams, incorporating changes made to the original files and distributing them to edge server 104 for future reference.
[0066] Together, client device 102, edge server 104, and cloud server 106 work together to ensure efficient management of video streams in 3D virtual environments. By dynamically adjusting the availability and resolution of video streams based on the user's camera view, they conserve bandwidth and computing resources, maintaining a seamless experience for the user while minimizing unnecessary data transfer and processing demands."

BACKGROUND ART

[0004] Conventionally, there are various methods of generating 3D animation images such as movies, television dramas, video games, and advertisements. Among them, it has been common to create 3D animation by manually operating a mouse while viewing a screen of a computer terminal. However, since this requires a lot of labor, the cost is also high. Therefore, in recent years, there have been proposals to generate 3D animation automatically without manual operation. For example, Patent Literature 1 discloses a system for automatically creating character motion from natural language sentences. Also, Patent Literature 2 discloses a system for automatically generating action animation of characters from a description file containing text describing actions. Furthermore, Non-Patent Literature 1 discloses a system for generating dance motions by machine learning. In addition, Non-Patent Literature 2 discloses a system for generating dance motions by deep neural networks.

However, in these conventional systems, the accuracy of generated 3D animation may not reach the level of actual human movements due to limitations in the modeling of human body dynamics or the like. Accordingly, even if a system can generate 3D animation automatically, there is still room for improvement in terms of quality. In particular, when considering the generation of 3D animation for advertising purposes, it is necessary to achieve both efficiency and high-quality results. This means that automation of the creation process needs to be further improved.
